claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a native oxide film on its surface.
The native oxide film passivates Q235 steel and acts as a protective barrier at room temperature.
At elevated temperatures, the native oxide film degrades or loses stability.
Thermal degradation of the native oxide film breaks down passivation and accelerates corrosion in harsh environments.
The integrity, thickness, and chemical composition of the native oxide film govern its protective effect.
Removing the native oxide film eliminates a protective barrier on Q235 steel.
At room temperature, oxide removal will increase the corrosion rate relative to oxide-intact Q235 steel.
Raising the exposure temperature from approximately 25°C to 60–80°C will increase corrosion in both oxide-intact and oxide-removed samples.
The oxide-intact samples will show a larger temperature-induced relative increase in corrosion rate than oxide-removed samples.
The larger relative corrosion-rate increase in oxide-intact samples will result from thermal degradation of the native oxide and exposure of reactive metal.
The proposed mechanism applies under high-humidity saline exposure at approximately 25°C and 60–80°C.
Conditions outside the stated humidity, salinity, and temperature ranges may produce different corrosion behavior.
Weight loss, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, SEM/EDS, and XRD can be used to compare corrosion and surface-film evolution between treatment groups.

A lack of statistically significant room-temperature protection by the intact oxide, or a lack of the predicted larger temperature-induced acceleration in untreated samples, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
